claims.text: Trace boron or silicon additions to tungsten promote grain-boundary segregation at 1500–1800 K.
Trace micro-alloying additions induce stable, thin amorphous intergranular films in tungsten at 1500–1800 K.
Amorphous intergranular films enhance grain-boundary sliding in tungsten.
Amorphous intergranular films impede crack propagation in tungsten.
The intergranular films govern the high-temperature plastic strain and toughness of micro-alloyed tungsten.
Controlled micro-alloying and an optimized heat treatment will promote and stabilize amorphous grain-boundary films.
Micro-alloying elements segregate to tungsten grain boundaries during processing.
Grain-boundary segregation leads to the development of amorphous intergranular films.
Amorphous intergranular films reduce the energy barrier for grain-boundary sliding.
Amorphous intergranular films distribute localized stress.
Reduced barriers to grain-boundary sliding and distributed stress enhance plastic deformation and toughness.
The proposed mechanism mitigates crack nucleation and propagation.
Micro-alloyed tungsten will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain than an undoped tungsten baseline.
Micro-alloyed tungsten will exhibit greater high-temperature toughness than an undoped tungsten baseline.
Effective formation of the films will produce a lower yield stress than in undoped tungsten.
Effective formation of the films will produce greater deformation before failure than in undoped tungsten.
The hypothesis applies to tungsten-based alloys at 1500–1800 K under vacuum or inert environments.
The mechanism may cease to apply above the thermal stability range of the amorphous films.
